item.title: The Week in Breakingviews: Appetite for disruption
item.description: What connects Elon Musk’s flawed assault on US government waste with the latest attacks on Riyadh Airport? Both are a reminder of the importance of a functioning state, and the risks of economic upheaval. Plus: the financial fallout in the Gulf, and praise for messy economics.
item.dc:creator: Peter Thal Larsen
item.content:encoded: Welcome back! A week ago I [USN:L6N45V0TR TEXT:"highlighted"] some of the cracks in the foundations of the AI boom. Those fractures have widened as debt investors fret about [USN:L6N4610VQ TEXT:"neocloud data centre operators"] and Anthropic reports [USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"slowing revenue growth"]. Temporary wobble or turning point? Email me with your views. If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend. OPENING LINE “The US commute is becoming an antique roadshow. Squeezed by high vehicle prices and borrowing costs, drivers are buying older cars with loans that last as long as eight years.” Read more: [USN:L6N44G18H TEXT:"The $1.7 trln auto loan market heads for a crash"] FIVE THINGS I LEARNED FROM BREAKINGVIEWS THIS WEEK The average price of an Anthropic token has dropped 68% since the start of 2025. ([USN:L6N4610VE TEXT:"The AI deflation trap"]) JPMorgan (JPM.N) added just $50 million to its allowance for consumer loan losses in the third quarter. ([USN:L6N45Z0W9 TEXT:"Jamie Dimon remains gloomy"]) Mukesh Ambani’s $102 billion Jio Platforms is set to go public on about the same valuation as rival telco Bharti Airtel (BRTI.NS) . ([USN:L6N45X01T TEXT:"IPO still makes sense"]) Qatar’s GDP is set to shrink by 16% this year. ([USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"But rebound in 2027"]) Dating app Bumble has a quarter fewer paying users than in 2024. ([USN:L6N45Z0WC TEXT:"AI to the rescue?"]) CREATIVE OBSTRUCTION In the US government they are known as bus people. These are the low-key functionaries on whom the state depends. “Bus people are people who if they are hit by a bus the government stops working,” a political operative states in Michael Lewis’s new book. Civil servants are the unlikely heroes of “ Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State ”, the author’s inside account of the assault on US bureaucracy by Donald Trump’s second administration and Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The tale is something of a departure for Lewis, who has previously tended to favour plucky underdogs taking on an entrenched consensus. Think of the sceptical fund managers of “The Big Short”, or the data-obsessed baseball administrators of “Moneyball”. A decade ago, Lewis might have been more sympathetic to the ignorant laptop-wielding twentysomethings dispatched by Musk to root out waste and inefficiency in the US bureaucracy. Instead, the short-lived DOGE debacle has helped draw a definitive line under a three-decade celebration of disruption as a positive force. The word used to have mainly negative connotations. Then the tech revolutionaries of Silicon Valley grabbed the public imagination. Harvard professor Clayton Christensen lauded the power of disruption in his 1997 book “ The Innovator’s Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail ”. Suddenly, everyone with a smartphone could be a business revolutionary. Technological evangelists preached the benefits of applying the same approach to the core functions of the state: education, healthcare, defence and so on. Looking back, the surprise is how little resistance they faced. Even the 2008 financial crisis, which exposed the extreme fragility of modern banking, only encouraged more reckless experimentation with cryptocurrencies. It took a global pandemic, a trade conflict, and the knock-on effects from actual wars in Ukraine and Iran to remind many citizens of the importance of basic administrative competence. At the same time, Silicon Valley revealed its reckless instincts, which are now on daily display with each leap forward in artificial intelligence. Consumers might welcome AI agents that help them [USN:L6N45N158 TEXT:"find cheap flights"], but are unlikely to tolerate rogue bots filing false homicide tips with Philadelphia police, as Anthropic [USN:L8N45V1NQ TEXT:"admitted last week"]. Back in 2016, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman [USN:L8N19F4MY TEXT:"put on jeans and visited California"] to show his determination to modernise the kingdom. Business leaders praised his disruptive vision. Yet it’s hard to attract $100 billion a year of overseas investment when Houthi insurgents are [USN:L6N45Y0GN TEXT:"blowing up Riyadh’s main airport"]. Even executives who shrugged off the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi will avoid the Saudi capital when their own safety is in doubt. This does not mean the government is necessarily efficient. Large sovereign debts and rising interest rates give politicians a strong impulse to seek more savings. The waves of “creative destruction” that Joseph Schumpeter described back in 1942 remain a feature of capitalist economies. Yet that system also depends on the state continuing to perform a wide range of everyday functions. It’s time we spent less of our attention on the self-professed disruptors, and more of it celebrating the bus people. CHART OF THE WEEK The latest war in the Gulf is doing serious economic damage. The leading economies in the Middle East are all set to shrink this year. The hope is that a peace deal will allow for a big bounce in 2027 as oil shipments resume and tourists return. Yet a prolonged conflict could undermine the region’s plans to reduce their dependence on fossil fuels, write [USN:L6N4600PN TEXT:"George Hay and Afiq Fitri Alias"]. Meanwhile, the gusher of investment cash is dwindling as current account surpluses shrink. THE WEEK IN PODCASTS Did you know that almost all our data zips around the world on 600 fibre-optic cables laid on the ocean floor, most of them no wider than a garden hose? Neither did I until I read Katja Bego’s “Deep Connections: The Hidden Battles to Control Subsea Cables”, a new book about this fragile underwater network. On The Big View we discussed how subsea cables evolved, how they have been weaponised in the past, and whether the modern global network can survive rising geopolitical tensions. Imported Chinese cars are the current focus of trade tensions with the European Union. Aimee Donnellan beamed into the Viewsroom from the Paris Motor Show this week to debate the cap on Chinese imports – and whether European carmakers can survive the onslaught – with Antony Currie and Katrina Hamlin. PARTING SHOT The main surprise about this year’s Nobel Prize in Economics was that the winners did not already have one. Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were instrumental in reconciling the two main schools of the dismal science into what became known as the New Neoclassical Synthesis. This paved the way for the distillation of major economic problems into three equations, and the proliferation of models which remain influential today. Yet theoretical elegance came at the expense of practical utility, [USN:L6N45Y0MG TEXT:"argues Jon Sindreu"]. Today, a messier approach probably allows for better policymaking. Want to receive The Week in Breakingviews in your inbox every Saturday? Sign up for the newsletter here . Follow Peter Thal Larsen on Bluesky and LinkedIn .

item.title: Hargeisa like a local
item.description: Our digital journalist’s guide to camel milk tea, bustling markets and mobile money.
item.dc:creator: Hani Richter
item.content:encoded: REUTERS/Illustration/Kate Evans “Resilience is victory,” goes a famous Somali proverb, and few places embody it like Hargeisa. Turned to rubble by intense bombings during a decade-long war with Somalia, this Somaliland city was rebuilt through domestic grit and community labour. Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991, is my home away from home. It is where my mother spent her early childhood and where some of my extended family still live. Though I was born in Bonn, Germany, and grew up in London, where I joined Reuters as a social media editor in 2019, I have regularly visited Hargeisa. Every time, I wish I had stayed longer. Hargeisa translates as “the place where hides are sold” in Somali, and livestock remains the backbone of the economy, alongside remittances. But it is also a city where old meets new: People buy and sell lambs and goats through their phones, using mobile money to pay for food, clothing and much else. Here’s how to experience Hargeisa like a local: Getting around: Somaliland is a devoutly Muslim place where days start early, with the first call to prayer before sunrise acting as a natural alarm for many residents. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. Everyone is in a rush, so be aware of your surroundings and be mindful of manoeuvring cars, buses, motorbikes and even the occasional determined man with a wheelbarrow. People shop at an open-air market along a street in Hargeisa, Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia that has enjoyed effective autonomy since it declared independence in 1991. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A Soviet-made MiG-17 fighter jet, formerly belonging to the Somali Air Force, sits atop the Hargeisa War Memorial monument in the Freedom Square along Independence Avenue. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader pours camel milk at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader handles camel milk from a steel can at an open-air milk bar. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man stands next to second-hand clothes for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traders wait for customers as they sell second-hand clothes. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman waits for customers at her open-air butchery. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A trader displays mobile phones for sale at an open-air stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Vehicles parked outside Durdur Business Center, along Road No 1, 26 June District. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman uses her mobile phone as she walks past the New Moon restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man uses a sewing machine at his tailoring stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Shoes are displayed for sale at the Kaboole fashion store. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A man sits inside the Muddakar coffee house restaurant. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed A woman sells fruit at an open-air grocery stall. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed People sit at a coffee shop. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed Traffic along a street in Hargeisa. REUTERS/Mohamed Ahmed For a more local experience, take a minibus. It’s a hail and ride system, so just flag down the bus as you would a taxi, confirm it’s going to your destination, and let the driver know when you want to get off. Note that they can often be crowded. For journeys outside of the centre, take a taxi or Dhaweeye, which translates as “closer” in English. They are always nearby and easily flagged off the street. Mobile money is king: As is the case in many African cities, mobile money is the preferred payment method in Hargeisa and to pay for anything you will need your phone. You don't need internet access; just ask which code to use and for the vendor's number. You can also pay with cash, of course, but it may take a bit longer. What to eat and drink: Many people make a living by selling their wares on the street. As you walk around the city, you will be called into restaurants and street stalls, where fruit sellers pile watermelons as tall as a person, and vendors fry potatoes. Camel meat and camel milk are must-tries. Somalis have been eating camel for centuries, a tradition rooted in the land’s arid landscape. When crops and cattle perished, camels were the only ones to survive. For a traditional snack on the go, try dried camel meat, called muqmaad. Walking is a great way to take in the atmosphere of the city. Though be warned: Roads and driving can be chaotic. For breakfast , people enjoy stir-fried goat, lamb or beef liver with Somali pancakes (lahoox), or a flaky flatbread with honey that goes well with shaax, a spiced, aromatic tea made with camel milk that tastes very similar to chai. A favourite lunch is fragrant Somali rice (bariis) and meat, typically tender, bone-in goat or lamb — with a banana on the side. Tea is at the heart of social life in Hargeisa, and you will regularly see people sitting outside tea houses, drinking and talking politics. With Ethiopia next door, you are never far from a good cup of coffee either. Try Social Cafe, one of several cafes in the city or, for a Somali twist, order Qaxwo, made with spices such as ginger, cinnamon and cardamom. City landmarks: The Hargeisa War Memorial features a downed Somali Air Force MiG-17 aircraft. Located in Freedom Square, it is probably the city's most recognisable landmark. The livestock market offers a glimpse into one of the city's main economic drivers, and is particularly interesting if you have never experienced the pastoral side of Somali culture. You’ll see large numbers of goats, sheep and camels being sold. Go in the morning to see it at its busiest. If you are looking for entertainment, stop by the Hiddo Dhawr Cultural Centre. Founded in 2013 by Somali singer and activist Sahra Halgan, it often features live performances of Somali music and poetry. For an authentic shopping experience, visit the Waheen Market, the city's main commercial market, where you will find everything from mattresses and glassware to gold jewellery. It’s also a great place to pick up a souvenir. One popular option is a dhill, a traditional wooden vessel used to store milk, usually adorned with leather straps and cowrie shells. Another is frankincense, an aromatic resin. Somaliland is one of the few places in the world where frankincense grows naturally. The gum is chewed for its health benefits, while the resin is traditionally burned to freshen homes and welcome guests. Finally, no visit to Hargeisa is complete without a trip to the money market, a famous open-air street market where vendors trade bricks of local currency and US dollars. There are piles of cash as far as the eye can see — but with mobile money now the first choice, who knows how long it will be there. Dress like a local: Hargeisa is a conservative place where people dress modestly. To fit in, try sporting some traditional dress. Women wear beautiful dresses called baatis with matching hijabs, often in tie-dye or other intricate designs, while men wear a sarong wrap decorated with traditional prints. When to visit: If you are visiting during the summer months, when it is hottest, expect average temperatures of around 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) during the day. In winter, temperatures reach about 26 C (79 F) at their highest, which is considered cool. CITY MEMO DATA POINTS Population : 1.3 million Price of a cup of tea : $0.20 to $1.50. My go-to spot for breakfast or lunch is CFC. Great place to watch the sunset : Sarovar Hotel is located at the top of a mountain and offers an unforgettable view of Hargeisa. Largest university : University of Hargeisa, more than 7,000 students

item.title: Chuck Lorre on his reign as the ‘King of Sitcoms’
item.description: The television writer and producer behind “The Big Bang Theory” and “Two and a Half Men” reflects on his career, the key to great comedy, and why he remains optimistic about television.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Serhan
item.content:encoded: American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole Laughter, Chuck Lorre is keen to point out, is not a voluntary act. It is not something we choose, but something that happens to us, like an unexpected gift. Lorre knows something about making it happen. Dubbed the “King of Sitcoms,” he has spent decades making audiences laugh, from his early work as a writer on the hit comedy “Roseanne” to creating shows, including “The Big Bang Theory,” “Two and a Half Men,” “Mom,” and “Mike & Molly.” In his newly released memoir, “Sitcom,” Lorre turns that comic instinct on his own life, writing candidly about his missteps, while also looking back at the television successes and creative battles that shaped his career. Speaking with Reuters from Los Angeles, he discusses why character is key to great comedy, what he learned from getting things wrong, and why he’s optimistic about the TV industry’s future. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. The memoir is very funny despite tackling difficult subjects, from failed marriages to addiction and Scientology. What made you want to open up about them now? From the outset, I was trying to write it as if I was having a conversation with somebody. Rather than reporting or reiterating stuff, I was trying to write it as if I was talking to the audience or talking to a person; more conversational as opposed to you know, being locked up in the prose of it all. I've been talking about these crazy chapters of my life for a long time and dear friend nudged me for at least two years to start writing it down. And once I started writing it down, I was quite pleasantly surprised. I realized it was cathartic. It was it was a little bit of therapy for me. Having finished the darned thing, what became really clear was all the missteps I've made in my life were all necessary for me to arrive at where I am, and I am deeply grateful for where I am. So the path may have been bumpy, but that's what was required. What most excites you about television right now, and what terrifies you? There's plenty in this world that is terrifying, but I wouldn't put TV in that category. Actually, I'm an optimist about how the business is changing. I've heard people complain that there's too many choices. And to me that's like, really? Does that mean when you walk into a supermarket, you complain that there's too many choices? That's got to be a good thing. When I came up in this in television, there was three and a half networks. Fox was just starting. And that was it. If those three said no, it's simply not going to happen. Now there's I don't know how many platforms capable of helping a writer (or) performer create something and perhaps get it seen by a legitimate audience. Of all the shows you’ve created, which felt most miraculous? Probably Big Bang. I mean, the first pilot was an abject failure, with the exception of (co-stars) Johnny Galecki and Jim Parsons. I had to wrap my head around the fact that it was poorly written and, when we were given another opportunity one year later, we got a chance to write a better pilot. You don't get do-overs in this business, but we did. Actress Kaley Cuoco along with the cast and writers of "Big Bang Theory" accept their award for favorite TV comedy at the 2010 People's Choice Awards in Los Angeles January 6, 2010. REUTERS/Lucy Nicholson I didn't understand what we were creating till we created it. I didn't understand how viscerally the audience was going to connect with these outliers, these brilliant but incompetent characters. What makes a great comedy? It's really very simple. It's about characters. Well-designed, thought out characters, portrayed by the right actor. I adored "Cheers" and "Seinfeld" and "Everybody Loves Raymond," "Archie Bunker," Norman Lear's stuff. I wasn't watching for the plot. The storytelling of it was secondary. It was these extraordinary characters that I loved and I wanted to see them every week. And that's how I've always approached creating television shows. Character, character, character. I don't think I could sit here and remember one storyline for "Cheers," but I never missed an episode because I wanted to see those characters. Those characters made me laugh. And I think that's the secret sauce for comedy. Obviously, when you work in the drama world, plotting is an entirely different thing. You're watching for the adventure, the hero's journey. That's a story. But even in that world, which I know very little about, I'm thinking about character. Going back to the importance of casting, you write about the resistance you faced casting Melissa McCarthy in “Mike & Molly,” with one network executive pushing for a slimmer actress. How much has the industry changed, and how did you learn which battles were worth fighting? The nominees for outstanding lead actress in a comedy series (L-R) Martha Plimpton, Melissa McCarthy, Amy Poehler and Edie Faco stand on stage as they congratulate winner McCarthy from "Mike & Molly" at the 63rd Primetime Emmy Awards in Los Angeles September 18, 2011. REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni Well, the good news is, because I've had some success, I don't have that many battles anymore. But it took a long time for me to fight for who I believed in as opposed to being a good soldier and taking direction. I learned the hard way that when you do what you're told to do by others and you fail, it's your failure. It's not theirs. At a certain point, I started to dig my heels in and I think first and most formidably (was) with Jon Cryer. I talk about how much resistance I got from CBS to cast Jon in "Two and a Half Men" and then Melissa McCarthy. Here was a generational talent and it was "over my dead body" kind of casting. And I went, "Fine, well, produce a dead body because we're going over it." I guess what I'm trying to say is, it took me a while to find the courage to fight these fights. I didn't have it in the beginning. I was too frightened about being tossed aside and sent home. American television producer Chuck Lorre poses for a portrait at Warner Bros. Studios in Burbank, California, US, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Cole How concerned are you about AI in the writers’ room? Are the protections won in the 2023 writers’ strike enough? There's plenty of reason to be concerned about this technology. Television would be the least of it, I would think. Why is that? I just think, if we're going to prioritize our concerns, for me AI is concerning in that it could topple civilization, not take away jobs on sitcoms, not that that's not important. But creating an intelligence that so wildly surpasses human intelligence is an incredibly risky endeavor. Look what we've done as the apex predator on this planet. Imagine what would happen if there was an apex-apex predator that viewed us the way we view insects. That scares me. Do you expect to see more shows tapping into those fears? We did an episode on "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" with an AI overlord that has shock collars around everyone so when they get angry or contentious and asocial, they're shocked into submission. You write that good TV writing starts with reading good writing. What happens to television if people are reading less? I really love words. I love the meaning of words, the sound of words, the music of words. And comedy, from my perspective, is really absolutely correct use of words to cause a response; to cause laughter. And laughter happens to you. Real laughter is involuntary. It should surprise the laugher. And that's a result of both words and images. I guess I could be concerned about a future where words become less relevant because they're my favorite things. Finally, some quick-fire questions. If you had to cast someone to portray you, who would you insist on? Idris Elba. No? Maybe not. (laughs) Why would you even ask that question? Are we going to make a movie out of the book? You never know! If you could revisit one of your shows, which would it be? "Dharma and Greg." I've always felt a profound regret for having left. There was so much more to explore, but I didn't know how. What’s your comfort watch? I really am drawn to dramas. I like to watch what I don't do. I love "Slow Horses" and "Furious." "Lucky" was another thing I saw and really enjoyed. "The Diplomat" is (also) terrific. As far as current comedies are concerned, if I want to laugh, I watch John Oliver and Jon Stewart. They absolutely know how to make me laugh out loud. The perspectives expressed in Culture Current are the subject’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views of Reuters News.

item.title: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital
item.description: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le pape Léon XIV est sorti de l'hôpital samedi après-midi pour regagner le Vatican, quatre jours après avoir subi une intervention chirurgicale pour un cancer du poumon. Le souverain pontife, âgé de 71 ans, s'est rendu sans aide jusqu'à la voiture qui l'attendait, s'arrêtant pour saluer les fidèles rassemblés devant l'hôpital Gemelli de Rome. Ses médecins avaient précédemment indiqué qu'il se sentait suffisamment bien pour rentrer chez lui après avoir effectué les dernières analyses sanguines et examens d'imagerie thoracique. Le pape, qui a subi mardi une opération visant à lui retirer le lobe inférieur du poumon droit, fera dimanche sa première apparition publique depuis son intervention pour prononcer la traditionnelle prière de l'Angélus sur la place Saint-Pierre, a confirmé le Saint-Siège. Léon a reçu un diagnostic d’adénocarcinome pulmonaire, la forme la plus courante de cancer du poumon. Ce diagnostic, pour un pape connu pour être relativement jeune et énergique et qui n’a été élu qu’en mai 2025, a provoqué un choc et soulevé des questions quant à l’avenir de son pontificat alors qu’il doit faire face à la maladie. Les médecins du pape ont indiqué que son opération s’était déroulée avec succès, sans complications. Ils n’ont toutefois pas encore révélé la taille de la tumeur ni précisé si la maladie s’était propagée aux ganglions lymphatiques voisins, deux facteurs essentiels pour établir le pronostic.

item.title: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after cancer surgery
item.description: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: A smiling Pope Leo left hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how his 17-month papacy might change. The pope walked unaided to his waiting car, waving to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment. Leo, 71, was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital grounds. He appeared in good spirits as he left the hospital in video released by the Vatican. He shook hands with a group of Franciscan friars, one of whom said: "This is the second time (we have met). Let's hope there will be a third and fourth." The pope laughed and replied: "Many times, but not for these reasons." PRAYERS ON SUNDAY His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Leo, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery when he will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims from his apartment overlooking St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT) on Sunday. He has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"raised questions"] about the future shape of his papacy. The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumour or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis. SOUTH AMERICAN TRIP Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said that Leo could be fully recovered in another 10 days and that there was no reason to call off his planned visit to South America next month. "As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," he told the Vatican News website. Leo is planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a pope [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Margaritora said the tumour had been discovered by chance during what he called a routine abdominal examination. The Vatican signaled on Friday that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the pope's health. In a sign the pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, [USN:L8N4621IK TEXT:"urging a ceasefire"] to help get vital supplies into Oleshky, a Russian-controlled Ukrainian town. Lebanese pilgrim Abdul Halim Fatha was in St. Peter's Square as Leo arrived back at the Vatican and expressed sadness over the pope's cancer diagnosis. "But I know God will be with him and protect him," he said.

item.title: Indian state food safety authority names Reliance, Blinkit executives in expired food probe
item.description: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi
item.content:encoded: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters. The Food and Drug Administration of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai, has led a [USN:L4N44Z0MR TEXT:"crackdown"] on food safety under its chief Tukaram Mundhe, 51, including shutting down some of Mumbai’s most popular eateries as well as outlets of Domino’s and Pizza Hut for poor hygiene. The state agency has also suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet. The latest case, which has led to a police complaint by the food safety authority, involves large retail and quick-commerce companies, which sell products to millions of households in the world’s most populous country. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, according to the documents reviewed by Reuters, said its officials visited some warehouses of Reliance Retail, Reliance Consumer and Zomato Hyperpure, and that company officials could not provide verifiable proof that disposal of expired food was actually carried out by their contractors. "The disposal agencies ... do not destroy the stock," the case document alleged. In the case of a Zomato Hyperpure warehouse, a company representative named a contractor as its disposal agency which FDA officials could not trace, according to the documents. Reliance and Blinkit did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Any attempt to divert expired, damaged or consumer-rejected food products meant for destruction back into the market is a serious matter that demands strict scrutiny and accountability," Maharashtra's FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters. "No company, brand, business or individual is above the law when it comes to food safety." INDIA'S INTENSIFYING CRACKDOWN Reliance Retail and Reliance Consumer are part of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s business group. Zomato’s Hyperpure is a unit of Eternal that also runs food delivery service Zomato and quick commerce business Blinkit. The FDA probe said it found a pattern where large retail and quick commerce distribution warehouses handed over expired and customer-rejected packages of food to contractors who passed the food to unlicensed sorting yards. These sorting yards then separated out saleable-looking packets, which eventually reached other retailers and the consumer market, according to case documents from the probe. "The chain thus runs from company warehouse to disposal agency, unlicensed yard, broker, retailer and consumer." The Maharashtra FDA on Thursday suspended the licences of five establishments in the state — three Reliance and two Eternal entities, the case documents said. Enforcement of food safety laws has traditionally been weak in India and the recent round of extensive crackdowns has garnered large-scale public support. In August, Indian authorities [USN:L4N44S18T TEXT:"raided"] an illegal operation in Mumbai that faked expiry dates and nutritional information on original food products manufactured by PepsiCo (PEP.O) , Nestle (NESN.S) , Coca-Cola (KO.N) and Unilever, so they could be exported to other countries. (This story has been corrected to say 'Reliance retail and consumer units,' not 'Reliance Group entities,' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
item.description: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030. Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act. Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery. He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion". Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"initial public offering"] expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion. HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control. "We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials. AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a [USN:L1N45Z01U TEXT:"source of growth"] offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash. Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind. But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants. More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said. STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology. "Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said. Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety." Despite some recent high-profile incidents where [USN:L4N45N1OZ TEXT:"rogue AI systems"] have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years." Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

item.title: India's HDFC Bank Q2 profit rises 4.7%; deputy MD Bharucha to step down
item.description: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Manikandan
item.content:encoded: India's largest private-sector lender, HDFC Bank (HDBK.NS) , reported a second-quarter profit on Saturday that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as weaker treasury income and higher provisions for bad loans offset strong lending growth. The lender also said in a regulatory filing that its deputy managing director Kaizad Bharucha will step down at the end of December. The news comes days before a leadership change at the Mumbai-based lender. Anup Bagchi, a veteran of the ICICI group, takes over as managing director and CEO for three years from October 27, becoming HDFC Bank's first external chief executive. Bharucha, who has been with HDFC Bank for over three decades, was one of two contenders for the top job, Reuters had [USN:L4N44R00C TEXT:"reported"]. Bagchi [USN:L1N45N0I6 TEXT:"takes charge"] amid increased scrutiny of the bank's governance, profitability and operational performance. The lender posted a standalone net profit of 195.10 billion Indian rupees ($2.05 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, compared with 186.41 billion rupees a year earlier. Analysts had estimated a profit of 195.26 billion rupees, according to data compiled by LSEG. Treasury trading gains fell to 7.8 billion rupees from 23.9 billion rupees a year earlier, weighing on earnings despite broad-based loan growth. Other income, which includes gains on bonds and other investments, fell 3.6% to 138.31 billion rupees. Indian lenders reported strong credit growth in the quarter across corporate and retail loans. HDFC Bank's net interest income rose 9.7% to 346.19 billion rupees, with total loans up 16.3%. Deposits grew 18.8% from a year earlier, and the credit-to-deposit ratio stood at 96.0%. Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies rose 2.1% to 35.74 billion rupees. Asset quality improved. The gross non-performing asset ratio was 1.11% at the end of September, compared with 1.17% at the end of June. ($1 = 94.9600 Indian rupees)

item.title: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure
item.description: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and ...
item.content:encoded:
Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 21:22 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 21:22 IST

US President Donald Trump (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy. Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation. The order provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18, but suspends their application through a presidential waiver. "Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the White House Executive Order stated. The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn, while existing Russia-related sanctions under other Executive Orders remain unaffected. According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), the decision provides India temporary relief but leaves open the possibility of Washington restoring tariff pressure during future trade negotiations. In its report titled "U.S. Waives Russian-Oil Tariffs: Temporary Relief for India, but Uncertainty Remains," GTRI said, "For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty." R Ramachandran, former Director (Refineries) at Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), told ANI that the immediate benefit for Indian oil companies would be greater crude sourcing flexibility rather than necessarily higher refining margins. "So more than the GRM, what actually impact it will have on Indian refineries will be the availability of more crude choices," he said. Gross refining margin (GRM) refers to the difference between the value of petroleum products produced by a refinery and the cost of crude oil processed. Ramachandran explained that increased Russian crude availability could help refiners secure more economical supplies, depending on discounts. However, lower crude prices could also be accompanied by falling petroleum product prices, limiting gains in refining margins. Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, said Russia's importance to India has increasingly shifted from discounted oil towards ensuring uninterrupted supplies. "The discount has really reduced significantly. But yes, what is more important for India now is availability and ensuring consistent supply of crude oil for the economy," Sinha told ANI. She said Russia's share of India's crude imports had exceeded 30 per cent in recent years, although its price advantage over international benchmarks had narrowed. GTRI noted that Russia's share in India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as purchases shifted towards the United States and the United Arab Emirates. The think tank also highlighted Washington's own energy requirements as a possible factor behind the waiver. According to its report, the United States agreed to purchase Russian diesel under an October 9 agreement to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices. It also noted that Washington had agreed not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that targeting India alone could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations. "The message is clear: U.S. interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said in the report. Meanwhile, Ramachandran said a sustained waiver could help reduce freight costs and ease logistical constraints associated with Russian oil shipments. He said greater vessel availability and smoother payment arrangements could improve crude procurement economics. "If Russia and India can agree upon on a continued ruble-rupee exchange for this, it also supports to ease the foreign exchange outgo which currently is affecting the Indian Rupee's strength," he said. However, these benefits would depend on the restrictions that remain applicable. On the broader economic impact, Sinha said India's current account deficit could remain manageable despite elevated crude prices, supported by merchandise and services exports. She expects the current account deficit to remain between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent of GDP, assuming crude prices range between USD 80 and USD 100 per barrel during the remaining financial year. However, persistently higher prices could widen the deficit towards 1.5 per cent of GDP under adverse conditions. Sinha expects average inflation of around 5 to 5.5 per cent, although higher fuel costs and food inflation remain risks. She said the fiscal impact would depend on whether elevated oil costs are absorbed through excise duty reductions, oil marketing companies or higher retail fuel prices. Healthy tax collections and potential disinvestment receipts, including from IDBI Bank, could help the government manage fiscal pressures, she added. On the rupee, Sinha said the waiver could improve market sentiment but was unlikely to provide substantial direct support to the currency. She also stressed that a lasting India-US trade agreement would offer greater economic stability than temporary tariff relief, warning that fresh US tariff threats could emerge. Ramachandran cautioned against immediately entering long-term Russian crude supply agreements without clarity on the waiver's duration. "The first thing I would say is that it is too early to look at jumping into long-term contracts," he said. He added that refiners would need to assess whether Russian crude discounts and stable supply conditions could be sustained. GTRI similarly warned India against making permanent trade concessions in exchange for temporary relief. "India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed U.S. pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," Srivastava said. (ANI)

item.title: Axis Bank Q2FY27 result: Profit rises 38% to ₹7,003 crore, misses estimates
item.description: Net interest income rose 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, while loans grew 23 per cent and provisions fell 52.2 per cent; other income declined 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indian private-sector lender Axis Bank reported on Saturday a quarterly profit that narrowly missed analyst expectations, as higher operating expenses and weaker other income offset robust credit growth and lower provisions.Axis Bank, the country's third-largest private bank by assets, posted a stand-alone net profit of ₹7,003 crore ($737.5 million) for the quarter ended on September 30, compared with ₹5,090 crore a year earlier.Analysts, on average, had forecast a profit of ₹7,124 crore, according to LSEG-compiled data.Other income, which includes earnings from bonds and other investments, fell 1.4 per cent to ₹6,531 crore.Rising bond yields and volatility in the rupee during the quarter weighed on treasury income at the Mumbai-based lender, tempering earnings even as lending expanded across segments.Banks across India reported strong loan growth during the quarter across corporate and retail portfolios.Net interest income grew 11.8 per cent to ₹15,371 crore, helped by a 23 per cent rise in total loans. Deposits increased 20.7 per cent from a year earlier.Provisions for potential bad loans and other contingencies fell 52.2 per cent to ₹1,694 crore.The gross non-performing asset ratio stood at 1.16 per cent at end-September, compared with 1.28 per cent three months earlier.

item.title: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
item.description: History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Small boat approaches, opens fire on LNG tanker off Yemen’s coast, says UK maritime agency
item.description: A UKMTO-reported security incident involving an LNG tanker off Al Mukalla highlights rising regional tensions. The event is linked to ongoing Houthi attacks backed by Iran, recent airport strikes in ...
item.content:encoded:
Small boat approaches, opens fire on LNG tanker off Yemen’s coast, says UK maritime agency A UKMTO-reported security incident involving an LNG tanker off Al Mukalla highlights rising regional tensions. The event is linked to ongoing Houthi attacks backed by Iran, recent airport strikes in Yemen, and broader diplomatic involvement from US and Israeli leadership. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 20:37 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 20:37 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations stated on Saturday that it had received a report concerning a security breach involving an LNG tanker positioned 140 nautical miles southeast of Yemen’s Al Mukalla. The tanker’s master reported that the vessel was approached by a small skiff carrying seven individuals, which fired two rounds towards the ship, UKMTO noted. The vessel's embarked armed security personnel responded by firing two warning rounds, compelling the approaching skiff to alter its course, while authorities have initiated formal inquiries into the security incident. Al Mukalla functions as the premier port metropolis situated along Yemen's southern coastline, positioned adjacent to the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea within the Hadhramaut Governorate. Resting upon a compact coastal strip framed by the Hadhramaut mountain range, the municipality lies approximately 480 kilometres east of Aden. Operating as the administrative seat of Hadhramaut, the city functions as a prominent centre for the fishing sector, encompassing fish-canning and fish-meal plants, alongside serving as an essential node for maritime commerce and energy supply logistics. In late December 2025, the Saudi-led coalition executed airstrikes on the harbour, targeting UAE-linked arms shipments following clashes involving the Southern Transitional Council (STC). Adding to the regional instability, Iran has aided Yemen’s Houthis with intelligence and tactical guidance in their recent attacks against Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, The Wall Street Journal reported. Former Israel Defence Forces (IDF) Iran researcher Danny Citrinowicz told the media outlet, “The connection is very, very strong on the operational level,” and described the relationship between Iran and the Houthis as one of “shared strategic interest that isn’t based on a client-patron relationship, but rather on strategic cooperation”. The conflict involving the Houthis, Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government has deepened in recent times, with the Houthis controlling the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. According to Al Jazeera, the Yemeni government and the Houthis exchanged strikes in Taiz Governorate, in which Yemen’s government-aligned forces claimed that 378 Houthi fighters were killed. Earlier on Friday, Yemen's government accused the Houthi militia of targeting Aden International Airport with two missiles that landed near a Yemenia Airlines aircraft preparing for take-off to Cairo, according to the country's Information Minister, Moammar Al-Eryani. In a post on X, Al-Eryani said Yemenia Airlines flight IY 612, en route from Aden International Airport to Cairo International Airport, was preparing for take-off when the airport was targeted. The missiles reportedly landed approximately 500 metres from the aircraft and around 100 metres from the centre of the runway. While Iran has reportedly backed the Houthis, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was asked whether Saudi Arabia had sought Israel’s help. He said, “There are barely any Middle Eastern states that aren’t asking us for help,” according to The Times of Israel. Israel and Saudi Arabia were considered close to reaching an agreement to normalise relations before the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. US President Donald Trump has said Saudi Arabia should accept Israel's offer to help in the fight against Houthi rebels, describing Israel's support to the country as “very helpful” amid escalating regional hostilities. (ANI)

item.title: Russia says it hit Ukrainian steel plants, power infrastructure and ships
item.description: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia said on Saturday it had carried out a large-scale overnight attack on Ukrainian and infrastructure targets including the country's largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih, and vessels using the Ukrainian port of Odesa. The plant is owned by steel giant ArcelorMittal , which [USN:L1N45H03O TEXT:"suspended"] operations there in September after a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Russia's defence ministry said the plant supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex. It said Russian forces had also hit an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front line. A cargo vessel in the Black Sea was also hit, the ministry said, alleging that it was delivering military cargo to Odesa. Later in the day, the ministry said Russian strikes during the afternoon had hit a vehicle-repair plant in Lutsk, an electricity substation in the western Ternopil region and another cargo vessel south of Odesa that it said was carrying military and dual-use cargo. Reuters could not independently confirm the ministry's reports.

item.title: Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery, recovery on track
item.description: Leo, 71, had greeted patients inside the hospital before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery, recovery on track

Pope Leo returns to Vatican after lung cancer surgery, recovery on track Leo, 71, had greeted patients inside the hospital before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle

Pope Leo waves as he leaves Gemelli Hospital following his lung surgery and cancer diagnosis, in Rome, Italy (Photo: Reuters)

AP Vatican City 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 8:28 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where dozens of well-wishers saw him off with cries of "Holiness."   "I am better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV. Leo, 71, had greeted patients inside the hospital before waving to well-wishers outside as he walked to the waiting vehicle. He briefly stopped when a teenage girl presented him with a homemade papal doll. His surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli, accompanied him to the hospital door as he was formally discharged.

Ten minutes after leaving the hospital, the pope entered the Vatican gates. He is due to greet the faithful with the traditional Angelus blessing on Sunday, a week after announcing that doctors had found a nodule on his lung. In an unusually candid disclosure, he said it would be removed. Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Also Read

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer, part of right lung removed, says Vatican

Antibiotic resistance emerging as major threat to surgical care: Experts

Pope Leo seeks strict AI rules, warns against profit-driven race

Marco Rubio urges Europe to act on Iran during Italy, Vatican visit

Marco Rubio discusses West Asia with Pope after Trump dispute

Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.

Medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon also described a good postoperative recovery, saying he had been able to carry on "normal daily activities completely on his own."   On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him in green vestments standing at an altar in the hospital chapel. Doctors said tests confirmed his "continued improvement."   Leo presided alone over the liturgy and distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. In his homily, he thanked hospital staff "for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him," Bruni said.

The Vatican had initially estimated a weeklong hospital stay and cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Experts said patients could be discharged earlier depending on their recovery, while Bruni said the decision rested with the pope's doctors. Leo's next major engagement is a trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17, giving him about three more weeks to recover before an ambitious journey that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter trips. The Vatican signalled that preparations were proceeding by publishing on Friday the names of journalists accredited to travel on Leo's plane. Oncology surgeons say patients are generally cleared to fly after three weeks, provided their recovery allows.

Doctors are still awaiting test results to determine the cancer's precise molecular and genetic makeup, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether further treatment is necessary.

item.title: India's space economy may reach USD 40-45 billion in 7–8 years, private investment key: Jitendra Singh
item.description: India's space economy is expected to grow from around USD 9 billion to USD 40–45 billion over the next seven to eight years, Union Minister of State for Space Jitendra Singh said on Saturday, ...
item.content:encoded:
India's space economy may reach USD 40-45 billion in 7–8 years, private investment key: Jitendra Singh India's space economy is expected to grow from around USD 9 billion to USD 40–45 billion over the next seven to eight years, Union Minister of State for Space Jitendra Singh said on Saturday, stressing that greater private investment, faster regulatory approvals and sustained commercial demand would be key to achieving this growth. ANI | Updated: 17-10-2026 20:21 IST | Created: 17-10-2026 20:21 IST

Union Minister Jitendra Singh speaking at a Roundtable organised by Bloomberg New Economy Forum (Photo/ANI). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India's space economy is expected to grow from around USD 9 billion to USD 40–45 billion over the next seven to eight years, Union Minister of State for Space Jitendra Singh said on Saturday, stressing that greater private investment, faster regulatory approvals and sustained commercial demand would be key to achieving this growth. Speaking at a media roundtable on "Space, Sovereignty and New Economy", organised by the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Singh said India must move beyond demonstrating technological capabilities to building globally competitive commercial space companies. According to a Department of Space release, the Minister stressed that "greater domestic and international investment, predictable demand, faster regulatory approvals and sustainable business models would be essential to scaling up Indian enterprises and expanding their presence in global markets." The projected expansion would make India's space economy nearly five times its current size, but achieving this would require private companies to develop commercially viable products and secure a steady customer base. Singh said the opening of India's space sector to private participation in 2019–2020 had produced significant results, but the next priority was to convert technological capabilities into sustainable businesses. Highlighting the importance of demand, the Minister said government institutions could act as anchor customers for private space companies, helping them develop and test technologies before commercial deployment. The release stated that "anchor government customers and support for proof-of-concept projects can help enterprises demonstrate their technologies and move towards commercial deployment." Singh also called for faster installation and export licence approvals, lower business costs and stronger supply-chain integration. He said GST-related reforms for space products must translate into practical benefits for businesses. On investment, the Minister emphasised attracting domestic and foreign capital while strengthening indigenous capabilities and maintaining strategic autonomy. He also highlighted the commercial potential of satellite communications, Earth observation and geospatial applications in infrastructure monitoring, agriculture, disaster management and defence. Singh said India's next phase of space-sector expansion would depend on combining private investment, predictable demand, efficient regulation and international partnerships to build globally competitive enterprises. (ANI)

item.title: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
item.description: A young lawmaker demands as new future as protests rage in Tirana.
item.dc:creator: Fatos Bytyci
item.content:encoded: Marjana Koceku's life changed last year when Prime Minister Edi Rama hand-picked her to run for Albania's parliament, one of a legion of young lawmakers he hoped would become the face of his Socialist Party. This week, however, the 25-year-old, now an independent member of parliament, joined [USN:L1N4610AQ TEXT:"mass student protests"] calling for Rama to step down. Corruption, a lack of jobs and a general feeling that the government does not work for them have created a deep-seated anger that spilled over this week, when young protesters swarmed the capital Tirana, setting fire to government buildings and banks and hurling pavement stones at police. The government and the police have condemned the violence. According to police figures, 500 protestors have been detained, 330 of whom have been released. Some 120 police and 45 protesters have been injured, the figures show, although the protester figure is likely higher given that many injuries have gone unrecorded. Albania's unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe, including in France, where high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities. YOUTH PROTESTS THREATEN RAMA'S RULE "The country is amazing, but ... the wrong policies that have been implemented by this political elite are completely against what the Albanian communities and Albanian citizens have been asking and seeking for so long," Koceku said during the protests on Friday as police fired tear gas and water cannon at protesters nearby. Rama, a former basketball player, has been in power since 2013, half Koceku's life. He won a fourth term in elections last year but his administration has since been dogged by corruption scandals. Rama denies wrongdoing and this week told Reuters that he would not step down. "Governments are changed through democratic elections and we had them last year, not through violence," he said. Still, the protests represent the biggest threat to his rule yet. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania's pristine southern coastline. The project, whose backers include US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, has faced legal challenges. Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was [USN:L6N42J18T TEXT:"wrongfully sold"] for the development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was [USN:L6N4380FB TEXT:"wanted by prosecutors"] on suspicion of drug trafficking, accusations his lawyer denied. Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute. He did not respond to requests for comment. That was not the only controversy for Rama's government. Last year, prosecutors alleged that his deputy prime minister was involved in [USN:L6N3ZC0BA TEXT:"doling out construction contracts"] to favoured companies, charges Rama and the deputy deny. "I didn't agree, especially with the policies that they were implementing against nature, and our land and our Albania," Koceku said. This week, protesters said they had resorted to violence because they had not felt heard. The Kushner-backed project upset Koceku, who has a close relationship with the land. She is from the remote mountains of northern Albania where her family runs a small, no-frills guest house on the shore of a lake. "Our country is the Albanian people," she said, the air around her thick with acrid tear gas. "They create the future, they create the now, and they are the ones who can bring our country forward. Not a single person, not a single government."

item.description: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Sisi says Egypt will not amend Constitution, rules out staying past 2030

Sisi says Egypt will not amend Constitution, rules out staying past 2030 Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023

Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi (File Photo)

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 17 2026 | 7:49 PM IST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.   The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general, the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs.   Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme.

Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed".   He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts. Also Read

The Mecca agreement is fuelled by regional concerns, say experts premium

Nine large banks engaged in so-called debanking, says US regulator

Jeffrey Archer, novelist whose real life rivaled his thrillers, dies at 86

Broadcom to lend Anthropic up to $42 bn to lease its chips, filing says

Iran bombing could ramp up after midterm elections: Donald Trump

"I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said.   The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months ??at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament.

Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030.   The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood - Egypt's first democratically elected leader - following mass protests.   He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.

item.title: インド警察、「ゴキブリ人民党」創設者を逮捕＝報道
item.description: [１７日 ロイター] -
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
[１７日 ロイター] - インドの複数のメディアは１７日、若者中心の団体「ゴキブリ人民党（ＣＪＰ）」の創設者アビジート・ディプケ氏が警察に逮捕されたと報じた。

テレビ局ＮＤＴＶとインディア・トゥデーによると、ディプケ氏は治安の混乱を防ぐために逮捕され、１７日に特別行政治安判事の前に出頭する予定だ。

同氏は拘束されたＣＪＰ幹部２人を支援するため、１６日にデリーで抗議集会を開くよう呼びかけていた。集会には数百人が参加し、国旗を振って選挙管理委員長の辞任を求めた。

ディプケ氏は１６日、デリー中心部の住宅から出たところを拘束され、短い口論の後、パトカーに押し込まれて連れ去られた。警察はこれに先立ち、ディプケ氏と面会し、抗議活動を実施しないよう警告していた。

item.description:
Milana Vinn
[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋 10/17 15:08 配信

ソフトバンクグループのロゴ。９月東京で撮影。REUTERS/Manami Yamada

Milana Vinn

[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの買収を検討している。関係者が１６日明らかにした。買収案では、アライドの評価額が約１８０億ドルになる可能性がある。

アライドは企業や各種施設、大規模イベントに警備員を派遣する事業を手がける。データセンター分野でも事業を拡大しており、施設の開発と運営の両面を支援している。

ソフトバンクはアライドの買収が実現すれば、特定の警備業務で人員の一部をいずれロボットに置き換えることを目指す。ただ人型ロボットの警備業務への導入には長い時間がかかるとみられる。

買収検討は初期段階にあり、買収額を含め、最終決定には至っていないという。

item.title: Strong dollar, weak hand for Trump before midterms
item.description: A surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants.
item.dc:creator: Jamie McGeever
item.content:encoded: With the US midterm elections weeks away, a surging dollar is exposing a central contradiction in President Donald Trump's economic agenda: currency markets are delivering the opposite of what his administration wants. Trump's economic record in the first two years of his second term is being heavily scrutinized. Polls show voters' approval of his handling of the economy has rarely been lower. That goes a long way toward explaining why [USN:L4N45Y17K TEXT:"betting markets "]point to his Republican Party losing control of the House of Representatives, and perhaps even the Senate, on November 3. Yet if there's any truth to the market adage that a country's currency is a reflection of the world's confidence in its economy, Trump should be going into the upcoming vote brimming with confidence. The dollar (.DXY) has been rising steadily, recently hitting its [USN:L4N46001K TEXT:"strongest level in 18 months"] against major peers. But a strong and appreciating exchange rate is the last thing Trump wants. His administration's economic and trade policies are aiming to revive US manufacturing, make American exports great again and shrink the trade deficit. A strengthening currency won't help with any of that. WRONG DIRECTION One might expect the dollar to be under pressure, especially given that the [USN:L1N45R0RR TEXT:"US trade balance"] has not narrowed according to the administration's plan. Imports have exploded to record levels, largely driven by US companies hoovering up the chips, equipment and goods needed for the AI build-out , and the country's trade deficit is widening. It was [USN:L1N45F0L5 TEXT:"2.7% of gross domestic product"] earlier this year — one of the smallest readings of the century — but it could be headed for 4% of GDP next year, according to Dean Maki at hedge fund Point72. But the dollar is not weakening. It did during Trump's first year back in the Oval Office, amid concerns about [USN:L1N44H0RB TEXT:""dollar debasement""] and a "sell America" mentality among foreign investors fostered by Trump's tariffs , but that has since gone into reverse. Why? Because exchange rates are relative, and the greenback currently appears to be the proverbial "cleanest dirty shirt." While the US is suffering from acute debt and deficit concerns, so are other developed countries, most [USN:S8N50E09F TEXT:"notably France"]. Investors fear that Paris is unwilling to take the politically unpalatable steps to get its budget under control and are thus slamming the euro . Similarly, worries that higher interest rates will make it nearly impossible for Japan to service its [USN:SPN45900X TEXT:"enormous debt load"] have anchored the yen near its recent historical lows. In short, the dollar is "winning" as much by default as it is benefiting from the flood of global capital chasing the US AI dream. This is not what the White House had in mind. Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent clearly [USN:L8N3YR24M TEXT:"want a weaker dollar"], even if decades of a quasi-official "strong dollar" policy at the White House — dating back to the days of former Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin in the 1990s — make it challenging for them to say so outright. The Trump administration's views on the US currency were flagged almost exactly two years ago in "A User’s Guide to Restructuring the Global Trading System," a paper by Stephen Miran, then a senior strategist at hedge fund Hudson Bay Capital Management. Miran went on to serve as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers under Trump, who later appointed him as a Federal Reserve governor for a short spell. He has since returned to HBC, but his 41-page manual still appears to serve as a broad framework for the administration's trade, currency and economic policy. The blueprint has come to be known as the "Mar-a-Lago Accord," in a nod to the famous 1985 "Plaza Accord," under which the world's leading economic powers agreed to devalue the dollar. Echoing Trump's decades-long view, Miran wrote that "deep unhappiness with the prevailing economic order is rooted in persistent overvaluation of the dollar ... (which) makes US exports less competitive, US imports cheaper, and handicaps American manufacturing." He has a point. At the time of Trump's inauguration in January last year, the dollar's broad, real effective exchange rate was the strongest in over 30 years. Miran argues that the global trade and financial systems can be rewired to America's benefit, but the path "is narrow, and will require careful planning, precise execution, and attention to steps to minimize adverse consequences." Americans casting their midterm election votes on November 3 may not have the patience for this. While the US economy continues to grow at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, households are feeling the adverse economic consequences of Trump's policies over the past two years. Tariffs have raised the cost of imported goods, according to a recent New York Fed study , and the US war with Iran, launched in February, has led to soaring energy costs, most notably record-high diesel prices at the pump. As a consequence, inflation remains elevated, bond yields are the highest in a quarter of a century, and real wages are now falling. Given all this, the big question is whether the American public will give the Trump administration the space to try to turn the dollar's tide. A FAREWELL TO MULTILATERALISM Efforts to reverse the dollar's march higher will be challenging, to put it mildly. History suggests that what's needed is multilateral, globally coordinated action, but that is the antithesis of Trump's "America First" worldview. Piecemeal and bilateral actions, like the Treasury's recent [USN:L4N45304A TEXT:"intervention with Japan"] to support the yen , are likely too small to have any lasting impact. Further interventions cannot be ruled out if the dollar continues to strengthen. For example, when writing about the yen, Stephen Jen, CEO of Eurizon SLJ Asset Management, recently argued that a series of targeted, surprise "mini" interventions could chip away at the dollar without triggering an avalanche of depreciation, helping the Trump administration meet its foreign exchange and wider goals over time. "The Trump Administration ... wants to find ways to guide the dollar lower. This is needed because, in order for the US to attain economic security, it needs to reclaim a certain level of manufacturing self-sufficiency. To do that, a weaker dollar would be necessary. The challenge, of course, is to guide the dollar lower without spooking the capital markets," Jen wrote in May. Much will depend on the frequency and size of such moves. Official action to weaken the dollar against major currencies is rare. Before this year's yen intervention, the last time US and Japanese authorities coordinated to sell dollars against the yen was in 1998. The Fed intervened with the European Central Bank and other authorities to support the euro, but that was back in late 2000, just after the single currency's launch. Since the era of free-floating exchange rates began in the early 1970s, when President Richard Nixon took the US off the gold standard, there have only been two truly global efforts to force a change in the dollar's broad value. Both were in the 1980s: the Plaza Accord in 1985 to lower what was an extremely elevated dollar, and the Louvre Accord in 1987 to essentially take the sting out of Plaza. These accords were products of their time. The dollar is nowhere near as strong as it was back then, and that was an era when multilateral cooperation was still in vogue. As the country looks set to enter the final two years of the Trump era, the dollar's relative strength could say much about how much of his economic agenda he has been able to achieve since first entering the White House almost 10 years ago. (The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary.
